title: Intro to Receptor Pharmacology
terms: ★ "What the BODY does to the DRUG": absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination (ADME). Basel: brief primer only; pharmacology covers it next year.
★ "What the DRUG does to the BODY": does it bind? what does it do when it binds? what systemic effects?
Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination: the four pharmacokinetic processes (Basel: "admi").
How (and how fast) the drug gets into plasma: oral (gut), intravenous injection, transdermal (skin), inhalation (lung capillaries).
Injection routes on the S6 figure; IV is easiest — "I put it in your plasma."
Absorbed through the stomach or small intestine; may need modification before absorption.
Absorption through lung capillaries (transcript; not on S6 figure).
Where the drug goes once in blood: bound vs free in plasma, fat (lipid) vs water, tissues A/B/C.
Distribution states on the slide: drug carried bound in plasma versus free in plasma.
Chemical processing by liver (or other tissues): glucuronidation, oxidation, sulfation, reduction, hydrolysis, conjugation.
Liver adds a big sugar (glucuronide) → more water-soluble → kidney excretes it. Basel's acetaminophen example.
How the drug exits: kidney filtration, bile, exhaled by lungs, sweated through skin (S5 diagram says "excretion").
Liver glucuronidates it → kidney filters and won't reabsorb it → washes out. Mechanism of action unclear (maybe "COX-3"). Overdose (~10,000 mg) lethal.
OUTSIDE — confirm: time for plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%. Listed on S4, NOT lectured (pharmacology next year).
OUTSIDE — confirm: area under the plasma concentration–time curve; total drug exposure. Listed, not lectured.
OUTSIDE — confirm: maximum (peak) plasma concentration after a dose. Listed, not lectured.
OUTSIDE — confirm: time after dosing at which Cmax is reached. Listed, not lectured.
OUTSIDE — confirm: lowest plasma concentration that produces the desired effect. Listed, not lectured.
OUTSIDE — confirm: not expanded on slides or in lecture; in anesthesia = minimum alveolar concentration.
OUTSIDE — confirm: lowest antimicrobial concentration that inhibits visible bacterial growth. Listed, not lectured.
Range between therapeutic and toxic/lethal doses; Basel uses it as the window the therapeutic index describes ("narrow window" for chemotherapeutics).
Does it bind to the receptor, and how well? → affinity, KD. In vitro, even cell-free.
When it binds, what does it do? → EC50, Emax. In vitro, on cells.
In a whole body, what systemic effects? → dose, ED50, TD50, LD50.
Cell-free study of affinity only — "does not care about any effects, just binding"; vary [drug] at constant receptor; Michaelis-Menten-shaped curve; described by KD.
Association rate constant: how fast the drug binds the receptor.
Dissociation rate constant: how fast the drug leaves the receptor.
★ KD = k-1/k1; drug CONCENTRATION (M) at which 50% of receptors are bound.
How tightly a drug binds. ★ LOW KD = HIGH affinity; high KD = low affinity. "Affinity isn't necessarily good or bad."
Binding curve follows Michaelis-Menten dynamics again: many open receptors → fast binding; as they fill, fewer binding events; 100% only at infinite concentration.
In vitro (cells): [drug] vs cellular effect; depends on binding + signaling; described by EC50 and Emax ("last lecture" = LC29).
Drug concentration (M) that elicits 50% of the maximal response in vitro.
★ Both ALWAYS have CONCENTRATION units. In a perfect world KD = EC50 (bind 50% → 50% response).
Mass/volume or moles/volume; needs a defined volume (petri dish, cell-free) — good for in vitro.
Mass/weight (mg/kg) or mass/surface area (mg/m²; slides: μg/m²); no need to know local concentration; PK comes into play. Better for in vivo.
Used for more dangerous drugs: toxicity scales better with surface area (squared) than weight (cubed).
In vivo: y = % of POPULATION responding as wanted; x = log dose; S-shaped curve; combines PD and PK; described by ED50.
★ Dose at which 50% of the population shows a therapeutic (positive) effect.
Dose at which 99% of the population shows a therapeutic effect.
★ Dose at which 50% of the population shows a toxic (negative side) effect.
★ Dose at which 50% of the population would be expected to die; ESTIMATED from side effects + animal studies, not dosed to death.
Dose at which 1% of the population shows a lethal effect.
★ Classic = LD50/ED50 (use unless otherwise defined). Larger = safer. ED50 ≈ LD50 → "not a drug, it's a poison."
★ Stronger therapeutic index: treat ~everyone before killing anyone. Want it > 1.
Amoxicillin, penicillin (>>100:1; ~100× dose without deaths). Allergy is a separate confounder (immune reaction).
Antifungal; fungi are "not all that different" from us → few selective targets → TI ~4; resistant fungi leave no room to raise dose.
Strong cough suppressant (not a pain reliever); TI ~15.
Narrowest TI: given by controlled infusion in hospital with close monitoring.
Strength of the response a drug produces (EC50); S21 compares potency of the response (EC50) with binding affinity (KD).
No spare receptors: 1:1 receptors to pathways (4 receptors, 4 pathways); response tracks % bound; receptor binding is the limiting step.
★ SPARE RECEPTORS: more receptors than pathways (8 receptors, 4 pathways); 50% bound → 100% response; signaling is the limiting step.
★ More receptors than signaling pathways; makes the cell more sensitive to drug and lets it survive receptor loss.
Critical receptors (adrenoceptors) — lose them and "you're basically dead"; reserve lets you absorb a toxin (e.g. snake bite) without losing max response.
Maximum response; lowered by an irreversible inhibitor only once the receptor reserve is gone.
★ Shifts EC50 RIGHT with full Emax (LOOKS COMPETITIVE) until the receptor reserve is depleted; then ↓ Emax.
Shifts the curve right (raises EC50) without lowering Emax.
Lowers Emax no matter the agonist dose; spare receptors can make it look competitive.
Adrenal tumor secreting catecholamines; surgical danger is hemodynamic instability from massive norepinephrine/epinephrine release.
Norepinephrine and epinephrine, released by the pheochromocytoma.
Smooth muscle receptor for catecholamines; many SPARE α-adrenoceptors in smooth muscle.
Irreversible, non-competitive α-adrenoceptor antagonist given pre-op; low doses look competitive (spare receptors); high doses toxic (narrow TI) → still used to "take the edge off."
Risk when massive epinephrine overwhelms low-dose phenoxybenzamine because receptor reserve is not depleted.
traps: PK vs PD: pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME); pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (binding, activation, systemic response). Don't flip them.
KD is a RATIO, not a difference: KD = k-1 / k1 (koff over kon). Off-rate on top.
★ Low KD = HIGH affinity; high KD = low affinity. Affinity is not good or bad on its own (transcript).
KD = binding (50% receptors bound) vs EC50 = response (50% of maximal response). ★ Both have concentration units (M).
Units trap: KD and EC50 = concentration (M, in vitro); ED50/TD50/LD50 = dose (slides μg/m²; Basel mg/kg or mg/m²).
Dose response y-axis = % of POPULATION responding (not % maximal effect); x = log dose (transcript, S15).
★ TI = LD50 / ED50 (lethal on top) unless otherwise defined; stronger version LD1 / ED99 (want > 1). Bigger = safer.
★ EC50 = KD → no spare receptors, binding limiting. EC50 < KD → spare receptors, signaling limiting. Never EC50 > KD for spare receptors.
★ With spare receptors, an irreversible antagonist looks COMPETITIVE (EC50 ↑, Emax kept) until the reserve is depleted, then Emax ↓. Opposite of LC29's "irreversible looks non-competitive."
Phenoxybenzamine: irreversible + non-competitive; fails at low dose (spare α-receptors); higher dose fails because its own TI is too small.
Glucuronidation = metabolism (PK), not elimination; the kidney then eliminates the glucuronidated drug (transcript).

know.note: ★ Basel's 4-vs-8 receptor thought experiment (Fri 11/6). EC50 < KD = SPARE RECEPTORS.

Potency of the response is greater than the binding affinity
Magnitude of response directly related to % receptors bound

quiz.stem: Which phrase from the lecture describes pharmacokinetics (PK)?
quiz.ok: What the body does to the drug
bad: What the drug does to the body
How the drug binds its receptor
What the drug does at the receptor
quiz.why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the pharmacokinetic ADME processes?
quiz.ok: Receptor activation
bad: Drug absorption
Drug distribution
Drug metabolism
quiz.why: ADME = absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination. Activation is a pharmacodynamic step.

quiz.stem: How is the dissociation constant (KD) defined from the rate constants k1 (kon) and k-1 (koff)?
quiz.ok: k-1 divided by k1
bad: k1 divided by k-1
k-1 minus k1
k1 multiplied by k-1
quiz.why: KD = k-1/k1, a ratio with the off-rate on top.

quiz.stem: Drug A binds a receptor with a dissociation constant (KD) of 1 nM; Drug B binds the same receptor with a KD of 100 nM. Which statement is true?
quiz.ok: Drug A has the higher affinity for the receptor
bad: Drug B has the higher affinity for the receptor
Drug A has the faster off-rate from the receptor
Both drugs have equal affinity for the receptor
quiz.why: Low KD = high affinity; low KD means k-1 (off-rate) is low.

quiz.stem: Which definition matches the dissociation constant (KD)?
quiz.ok: Drug concentration at which 50% of receptors are bound
bad: Drug concentration eliciting 50% of maximal response in vitro
Drug dose at which 50% of the population responds therapeutically
Drug dose at which 50% of the population shows lethality
quiz.why: KD = concentration (M) at 50% receptor occupancy; the others are EC50, ED50, LD50.

quiz.stem: A researcher adds increasing amounts of drug to a constant amount of receptor in a cell-free system and plots [DR] against [D]. What does this study measure?
quiz.ok: Affinity of the drug for the receptor
bad: Magnitude of the drug's cellular response
Percent of population with an effect
Toxicity of the drug in the animal
quiz.why: A binding study measures affinity (KD) and does not care about effect.

quiz.stem: A researcher treats cultured cells with increasing drug concentrations and plots concentration against the cellular effect. Which study and parameter is this?
quiz.ok: Concentration response study described by EC50
bad: Binding study described by the KD value
Dose response study described by the ED50 value
Dose response study described by the TD50 value
quiz.why: In vitro, drug concentration vs cellular effect = concentration response study, described by EC50 (M).

quiz.stem: Which parameter is paired with the unit shown for it on the lecture slides?
quiz.ok: ED50 in micrograms per square meter
bad: EC50 in micrograms per square meter
KD in micrograms per square meter
LD1 in moles per liter of plasma
quiz.why: KD and EC50 are concentrations in M; ED50 is a dose in μg/m2.

quiz.stem: Why is dose, rather than concentration, the better measurement for in vivo studies?
quiz.ok: Drug concentration at the receptor in the body is impractical to measure
bad: Dose measurements remove all pharmacokinetic influences on the response
Dose measurements require knowing the local concentration at the receptor
Concentration can only be expressed as mass per unit of surface area
quiz.why: Dose does not need absolute or local concentration, but it brings PK principles into play.

quiz.stem: A dose response study in a population of dogs depends on which combination of effects?
quiz.ok: Binding, signaling, and pharmacokinetic effects
bad: Binding and signaling effects, but not pharmacokinetics
Binding effects only, without signaling or pharmacokinetics
Pharmacokinetic effects only, without binding or signaling
quiz.why: Dose response studies combine PD and PK: binding, signaling, and PK effects.

quiz.stem: How is the therapeutic index (TI) defined on the slides?
quiz.ok: LD50 divided by ED50
bad: ED50 divided by LD50
TD50 divided by LD50
LD50 minus the ED50
quiz.why: TI = LD50/ED50, a comparison of doses; larger = safer.

quiz.stem: Based on the approximate therapeutic indexes on the slides, which drug has the narrowest margin between therapeutic and lethal doses?
quiz.ok: Cisplatin
bad: Digoxin
Cocaine
Morphine
quiz.why: Cisplatin 1.5:1 < digoxin 2:1 < cocaine 15:1 < morphine 70:1.

quiz.stem: For an agonist, the EC50 is lower than its dissociation constant (KD). What does this suggest about the system?
quiz.ok: There are more receptors than signal pathways
bad: There is a 1:1 ratio of receptors to pathways
Receptor binding is the limiting step in signaling
Response magnitude equals the percent of receptors bound
quiz.why: EC50 < KD = spare receptors; signaling, not binding, is limiting.

quiz.stem: For an agonist, the EC50 equals its dissociation constant (KD). Which step is limiting in the signal pathway?
quiz.ok: The receptor binding event
bad: The downstream signaling event
The drug absorption event
The drug metabolism event
quiz.why: EC50 = KD: response tracks receptors bound, so binding is the limiting step.

quiz.stem: A tissue has spare receptors. A low dose of an irreversible antagonist is added before the agonist curve is repeated. What happens to the agonist curve?
quiz.ok: It shifts right with no drop in maximal effect
bad: Maximal effect drops with no rightward shift
It shifts left with no drop in maximal effect
Maximal effect rises and the curve shifts left
quiz.why: With receptor reserve, full effect persists despite some irreversible inhibitor; non-competitive looks competitive.

quiz.stem: A dog with a pheochromocytoma receives low, tolerable doses of phenoxybenzamine before surgery, yet massive epinephrine release still causes a hypertensive crisis. Why?
quiz.ok: The spare alpha-adrenoceptor reserve is not depleted
bad: Phenoxybenzamine binds alpha-adrenoceptors reversibly
Epinephrine displaces phenoxybenzamine from receptors
Phenoxybenzamine is a competitive alpha antagonist
quiz.why: Spare α-adrenoceptors exist in smooth muscle; low-dose phenoxybenzamine (irreversible, non-competitive) does not fully deplete the reserve.

quiz.stem: In the same pheochromocytoma case, why is the phenoxybenzamine dose not simply raised until all alpha-adrenoceptors are blocked?
quiz.ok: Its therapeutic index is too small
bad: Its affinity for alpha receptors is too low
Its EC50 is lower than its KD value
Its effect is purely pharmacokinetic
quiz.why: Full blockade causes substantial toxicity that outweighs the benefit; the TI is too small.

quiz.stem: Which statements about spare receptors are correct? (select all that apply)
ok: They let a pathway signal fully despite some irreversible inhibitor
They can make a non-competitive antagonist look competitive
bad: They make the EC50 greater than the KD for an agonist
They make receptor binding the limiting step in signaling
They prevent an irreversible inhibitor from ever lowering Emax
quiz.why: Reserve keeps full signaling and masks non-competitive inhibition; once reserve is gone, Emax falls. Spare receptors give EC50 < KD and signaling is limiting.

quiz.stem: A dog receives acetaminophen. The liver adds a glucuronide group, and the kidney then excretes the more water-soluble product. Which branch of pharmacology describes these events?
quiz.ok: Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to the drug
bad: Pharmacodynamics: what the drug does to the body
Pharmacodynamics: how the drug binds its receptor
Pharmacokinetics: what the drug does at its receptor
quiz.why: Glucuronidation (metabolism) and renal excretion (elimination) are ADME = pharmacokinetics.

quiz.stem: How is LD1/ED99 defined, and what value suggests a good drug?
quiz.ok: Dose killing 1% over dose treating 99%; above 1
bad: Dose killing 99% over dose treating 1%; above 1
Dose killing 1% over dose treating 99%; below 1
Dose treating 1% over dose killing 99%; below 1
quiz.why: LD1 = 1% lethal; ED99 = 99% therapeutic. LD1/ED99 > 1 means you can treat nearly everyone before killing anyone.

quiz.stem: Drug P has a therapeutic index (LD50/ED50) of 70. Drug Q has a therapeutic index of 4. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Drug P has the wider margin and is generally safer
bad: Drug Q has the wider margin and is generally safer
Drug P is more potent because its index is larger
Drug Q is more efficacious because its index is smaller
quiz.why: Larger TI = bigger gap between effective and lethal doses = generally safer. TI says nothing about potency or efficacy.

quiz.stem: A snake toxin irreversibly blocks half of a tissue's alpha-adrenoceptors, which have a large receptor reserve. What happens to the epinephrine response curve?
quiz.ok: EC50 shifts right while Emax is preserved
bad: Emax falls while EC50 stays the same
EC50 shifts left while Emax is preserved
Emax falls and EC50 shifts to the left
quiz.why: With spare receptors, an irreversible antagonist looks competitive (right shift, full Emax) until the reserve is depleted. Basel: spare receptors let you survive toxins.

quiz.stem: A drug fills 50% of a receptor population at 10 nM in a cell-free binding study. Which statement about this value is correct?
quiz.ok: It is the KD, a concentration describing affinity
bad: It is the EC50, a concentration describing potency
It is the ED50, a dose describing effectiveness
It is the KD, a rate constant describing koff
quiz.why: KD = concentration binding 50% of receptors (binding study, affinity), always in concentration units.

flags: Slide citation typos
S25–S27 citation reads "Goodman & Gliman's The Pharmacologicalf Basis of Therapeutics" · correct title is Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics (OUTSIDE); typo only.
S4 PK terms not lectured

S4 lists half-life, area under the curve, Cmax, MEC, MAC, MIC, Tmax, therapeutic window; Basel gave only a PK "primer" (ADME) and said pharmacology covers PK next year · definitions here are OUTSIDE; likely low-yield for Exam 4.
MAC meaning unclear
S4 lists "MAC" with no expansion; not mentioned in lecture · anesthesia usage = minimum alveolar concentration (OUTSIDE).
CLOSED by transcript (Wed 11/4): Michaelis-Menten (S8)
Basel: the binding curve is "Michaelis-Menten dynamics again" (fast binding with many open receptors, then fewer binding events); same shape as LC29 · no math expected.
CLOSED by transcript (Wed 11/4): "LAST LECTURE" on S11
Basel: concentration response = "what we talked about last lecture" (LC29 EC50/Emax) · no old-numbering issue.
CLOSED by transcript (Fri 11/6): "KD is similar to EC50" (S10) vs EC50 < KD (S21)
Basel: "in a perfect world, KD and EC50 should be the same"; with spare receptors EC50 < KD · similar definition format, equal only without spare receptors.
Low KD = low k-1 AND high k1 (S10)
S10 says low KD means k-1 low and k1 high; Basel only said low KD = binds efficiently · OUTSIDE: KD is a ratio, so either change alone can lower it; use slide wording.
CLOSED by transcript: Excretion (S5) vs Elimination (S4, S6)
Basel: "E is elimination" (kidney, bile, lungs, skin) · use elimination for ADME.
Dose units: μg/m² (slides) vs mg/kg or mg/m² (Basel)
S15–S19 give ED50 in μg/m²; Basel said dose = mass/mass (mg/kg) or mass/surface area (mg/m², for more dangerous drugs) · keep slide units (μg/m²) for the exam; know both forms are "dose."
CLOSED by transcript (Wed 11/4): S9 stop-and-think — does an antagonist have a KD?
Antagonists bind → have a KD. Basel (LC29 part, Wed 11/4): antagonists have no efficacy or potency on their own → no EC50 of their own · agonist: KD + EC50; antagonist: KD only.
Figures checked against slide images

S17 values confirmed (ED50 ~5, LD50 ~10000, TI ~2000 μg/m²); S16 order ED50 < TD50 < LD50; S22 effect curve left of % bound curve with spare receptors, overlapping without; S23: spare + irreversible antagonist = right shift, full Emax; no spare ++irreversible = Emax ~35%.
Transcript slip: ADME under "pharmacodynamics"

Basel: "when we talk about pharmacodynamics, we can use this little crazy word called admi" (and "grew up living and breathing pharmacodynamics" re: dad in pharmacokinetics) · ADME = PHARMACOKINETICS (S4, S6).
Transcript slip: "no spare receptors, EC50 much less than KD"
During the snake-toxin example Basel says "if we have no spare receptors, our EC50 is much less than our KD" · S21–S22: EC50 < KD = WITH spare receptors.
Transcript slip: "ED99 over LD1"
Basel once says "ED 99 over LD1" then corrects to LD1 over ED99 · use LD1/ED99 (lethal on top, like LD50/ED50).
Acetaminophen mechanism (Basel unsure)
Basel: "might be a COX-3 inhibitor ... we're not entirely sure" · not testable as mechanism; the PK example (glucuronidation → kidney) is the point.
